The brushless motor controller experienced acoustic vibration and phase current distortion during closed-loop FOC commutation. We inspected the current sensing pipeline using a logic analyzer and identified phase alignment errors in the field-oriented control registers. The firmware samples the analog current shunts using three simultaneous ADC conversions, but the trigger event was misaligned with the center of the PWM cycle. To resolve this timing discrepancy, we configure the advanced timer by setting center-aligned mode 3 and route the counter overflow event directly to the ADC trigger input.

Next, we diagnosed the coordinate transform calculations inside the inner current loop. The rotor electrical angle from the quadrature encoder was lagging the stator flux vector by 20 degrees because the software omitted encoder filter delay compensation. We updated the Park transform input register by writing the compensated angle value 0x200 instead of the raw encoder reading.

We also adjusted the complementary output dead-time to 128 clock cycles in the dead-time generator register to prevent shoot-through currents in the inverter half-bridges. After updating the registers, phase currents returned to clean sinusoidal waveforms during high-torque operation.

Our automotive gateway was logging intermittent form error and bit error flags on the CAN-FD bus when switching from nominal arbitration to fast data phase transmission. We probed the CAN differential bus lines and discovered that the transmitter delay compensation loop was misconfigured. The nominal bitrate operates at 500 kilobits per second, while the data phase switches to 4000 kilobits per second by asserting the BRS bit in the message header. At 4 megabits per second, the physical transceiver propagation delay exceeds one bit time, causing the controller to sample its own transmitted bit during data arbitration.

To correct the timing mismatch, we configure the transmitter delay compensation control register by enabling the TDC unit and setting the secondary sample point offset to 16 time quanta instead. We measured the transceiver loop delay using an oscilloscope and verified that the hardware delay measurement matches 60 nanoseconds.

Write the measured delay value into the TDC filter register to reject spurious ringing pulses on the receive comparator line. This register adjustment restored reliable bit reception across all electronic control unit nodes without frame aborts during burst communication.

On the nRF52 SoC, we investigated radio packet timing jitter during high duty cycle BLE mesh transmission. When handling radio events using software interrupt service routines, the NVIC interrupt latency varied between 4 microseconds and 12 microseconds, depending on whether lower-priority peripheral interrupts were active. This jitter caused packet collisions during scheduled advertising intervals. To eliminate interrupt latency completely, we rearchitected the radio sequencing by routing radio events through the programmable peripheral interconnect rather than the CPU.

We configure PPI channel 0 by connecting the radio READY event to the radio START task, allowing the transmitter to ramp up and transmit the payload autonomously. We also bound PPI channel 1 to the radio END event to trigger a hardware timer capture task precisely when the CRC check completes.

For buffer management, we kept an NVIC interrupt on the radio DISABLED event with priority 0 in the NVIC priority register to reload the packet pointer before the next connection slot. This hardware event routing reduced packet timing jitter to under 1 microsecond and freed CPU cycles for cryptographic mesh packet computation.

Our embedded telemetry logger suffered from intermittent hardware watchdog resets during high-volume flash memory logging under FreeRTOS. We analyzed the crash dump and discovered that the windowed watchdog timer triggered an unmaskable system reset because the supervisor task refreshed the counter outside the permitted time window. The hardware watchdog was configured with a total timeout period of 1000 milliseconds and an upper refresh window of 600 milliseconds instead. Under normal conditions, the supervisor thread wakes up every 300 milliseconds to write the refresh key 0xAAAA into the watchdog key register.

However, when the flash filesystem flushed metadata blocks over the shared SPI bus, the high-priority storage thread preempted the supervisor task for over 700 milliseconds. This preemption prevented the supervisor task from servicing the counter before it decremented below the lower window boundary.

We resolved the watchdog timeouts by setting up a dedicated hardware timer callback to monitor the supervisor task health flags and feed the watchdog counter from interrupt context. We also write 0x5555 into the watchdog access register to update the window threshold to 800 milliseconds, providing sufficient timing margin during heavy flash write operation.

Route the issue down to DMA FIFO underruns between the circular memory buffer and the I2S serializer peripheral. Write 0x03 into the DMA control register to enable both half-transfer and transfer-complete interrupts with elevated NVIC priority. This double-buffering scheme guarantees that the audio hardware alternates seamlessly between memory buffers without pops or latency during continuous playback operation.

During field-oriented control tuning of our high-speed brushless motor drive, we observed severe current ripple and torque oscillations under heavy load. We investigated the three-phase current sensing circuitry and discovered that the analog-to-digital converter sampled the low-side shunts during the active switching transitions rather than the middle of the low-side freewheeling vector. This timing error corrupted the measured phase currents, causing the Clarke and Park transform algorithms to compute erroneous direct and quadrature axis current vectors.

To fix the sampling window, we configure the master timer by setting center-aligned mode 2 in the timer control register. Write the repetition counter to 1 so the timer generates a trigger event on every underflow when the bottom switches are conducting. We route the timer trigger output to the dual ADC injected channels by setting the external trigger selection bits 0x04 in the ADC control register.

We also updated the current sampling settling delay to 30 clock cycles in the sampling time register to avoid switching noise. After synchronizing the ADC conversions, phase current measurements stabilized and the motor delivered smooth torque across the entire speed range without commutation errors.

We analyzed the I2C bus capture with a logic analyzer and found that the supervisor firmware polled the regulators too slowly, allowing temperatures to exceed 85 degrees Celsius before tripping the overtemperature fault register.

This unmasks the thermal warning threshold interrupt on the dedicated SMBus alert hardware line. When the regulator junction temperature exceeds 75 degrees Celsius, the chip pulls the alert line low, triggering an NVIC external interrupt on the supervisor CPU.

We write command 0x0C to query the alert response address and retrieve the faulted node address 0x5A. This interrupt-driven fault scheme cut thermal fault response time from 500 milliseconds to under 2 milliseconds during high-power converter operation.

During field testing of our industrial motor drive, we encountered severe packet reception failures on the CAN-FD bus during high-speed data phase commutation. The controller communicates at a nominal bitrate of 500 kilobits per second and switches to 2000 kilobits per second for payload transmission. When multiple nodes transmitted simultaneously, the CAN core logged protocol error flags and entered error-passive state. We connected a protocol analyzer to the bus lines and discovered that the transmitter delay compensation secondary sample point was positioned too close to the bit edge.

The default configuration placed the secondary sample point at 50 percent of the bit time, but the physical isolation optocouplers introduced 70 nanoseconds of propagation delay, causing the receiver to sample ringing transients. To resolve the error frames, we configure the transmitter delay compensation register by setting the secondary sample point offset to 18 time quanta instead.

Write 0x18 into the TDC control register to enable the delay compensation filter and ignore glitch pulses shorter than 12 nanoseconds. This hardware filtering and sample point adjustment restored error-free frame reception across all nodes during high-speed motor drive operation.
